title: Phaedrus
author: Plato
openingText: SOCRATES: My dear Phaedrus, where are you coming from, and where are you going? PHAEDRUS: I'm coming from Lysias, the son of Cephalus, and I'm off to take a walk outside the city wall. I've been sitting with him all morning, and our mutual friend Acumenus tells me it's much more refreshing to walk in the open air than to be cooped up indoors.
about:
Phaedrus is a dialogue between Socrates and a young man named Phaedrus who has just heard a speech by the orator Lysias about love. They walk to a shady spot along the river Ilissus, where Phaedrus reads the speech aloud, Socrates responds with two speeches of his own — the second a soaring account of the soul as a winged chariot drawn toward divine beauty — and the conversation turns to the nature of rhetoric, the difference between true and false persuasion, and the superiority of living speech over written words.

Written around 370 BC, probably in the same period as the Republic and the Symposium, the Phaedrus is one of Plato's most formally inventive dialogues. It is the only dialogue set entirely outside the walls of Athens — the countryside setting matters, because what Socrates says about love, beauty, and inspiration is inseparable from the sensuous landscape in which he says it. The dialogue contains Plato's most celebrated myth (the chariot of the soul), his most sustained account of erotic love as a path to philosophical knowledge, and his most provocative argument against writing — delivered, of course, in writing. It is one of the foundational texts of Western aesthetics and rhetoric.

angleCards.title: Love as a philosophical force.
angleCards.text: Socrates's second speech argues that erotic madness — being overwhelmed by the beauty of another person — is not a disease but a divine gift that can lift the soul toward truth. Track how he turns an argument against love into an argument for it.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the Phaedrus as Plato's most passionate defense of eros — the argument that love is not a distraction from philosophy but the engine of it.

angleCards.title: The myth of the chariot.
angleCards.text: Socrates describes the soul as a charioteer driving two winged horses — one noble, one unruly. The myth is an image of what it feels like to want contradictory things at once. Watch how the image does philosophical work that abstract argument cannot.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to understand Plato's chariot myth as his account of the divided self — how desire, reason, and spirit pull in different directions and what it takes to hold them together.

angleCards.title: What makes rhetoric real?
angleCards.text: The second half of the dialogue asks what separates genuine persuasion from manipulation. Socrates argues that a true rhetorician must know the truth about the subject and the soul of the listener. Notice how this standard rules out most of what passes for public speech.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the Phaedrus for its theory of rhetoric — what Socrates thinks persuasion requires and why most speech fails the test.

angleCards.title: Writing versus living speech.
angleCards.text: Socrates tells a myth about the Egyptian god Theuth, who invented writing and was told by the king that it would produce forgetfulness, not wisdom. The argument is that written words cannot answer questions or defend themselves. Plato is writing this down — the irony is deliberate.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow Plato's critique of writing — his argument that the written word is inferior to living conversation — and decide what it means that he chose to write it.

cast.name: Socrates
cast.description: The central speaker, barefoot and apparently immune to the summer heat until he reaches the shade of a plane tree. He begins by mocking Lysias's speech on love, then delivers two of his own — the second an ecstatic vision of the soul's journey toward divine beauty. He is at his most poetic and most paradoxical in this dialogue: a man who distrusts rhetoric producing the most rhetorical speech in Plato's corpus.

cast.name: Phaedrus
cast.description: A young Athenian who has just come from hearing Lysias speak and is carrying the text of the speech under his cloak. He is an admirer of fine words and an eager audience — the kind of person who can be moved by a beautiful speech without asking whether it is true. Socrates's task in the dialogue is partly to teach Phaedrus the difference between being impressed by language and being changed by it.

cast.name: The Chariot of the Soul
cast.description: Socrates's image of the soul as a charioteer driving two winged horses — one white and noble, drawn upward toward beauty and truth, one dark and unruly, dragging downward toward appetite. The chariot myth is Plato's most vivid account of inner conflict and the possibility of transcendence. It does the work in this dialogue that the Allegory of the Cave does in the Republic.

cast.name: Lysias
cast.description: A famous Athenian speechwriter whose speech on love — arguing that a boy should favor a non-lover over a lover, because the non-lover is more rational — starts the entire dialogue. Lysias never appears in person; his speech is read aloud by Phaedrus. Socrates treats it as a case study in clever but philosophically empty rhetoric.

cast.name: Theuth and Thamus
cast.description: Egyptian god and king from the myth Socrates tells near the end. Theuth invents writing and presents it as a gift to memory; King Thamus replies that it will produce forgetfulness instead, since people will rely on external marks rather than internal understanding. The myth carries Plato's most direct statement about the limits of the written word.

whyItMatters.title: The Soul Has Wings
whyItMatters.body: The Phaedrus contains Plato's most sustained and most beautiful account of what it means to fall in love — and his argument that this experience is not a distraction from the pursuit of truth but the very thing that makes it possible. The chariot myth presents erotic desire as a recollection of divine beauty, something the soul once knew before birth and recognizes again in the beauty of another person. This idea — that love is a form of knowing, that beauty is a clue to something real — runs through Western thought from Augustine's Confessions through Dante's Beatrice to the Romantic poets. Every subsequent writer who has treated love as something more than appetite and less than delusion is working, knowingly or not, in the space Plato opened in this dialogue.

whyItMatters.title: The First Theory of Rhetoric
whyItMatters.body: The second half of the Phaedrus is the founding text of rhetorical theory — the first sustained attempt to distinguish genuine persuasion from manipulation. Socrates argues that a true rhetorician must know the truth about the subject, must understand the different kinds of soul in the audience, and must match the right kind of speech to the right kind of listener. This is not a manual of technique; it is a philosophical argument that rhetoric without knowledge is empty and dangerous. Every subsequent debate about public speech, propaganda, advertising, and political communication — the question of whether persuasion can be separated from truth — begins here.

whyItMatters.title: Plato Against Writing
whyItMatters.body: The Phaedrus contains the most famous critique of written communication ever produced — and the irony that it was written down is part of the point. Socrates argues that writing creates an illusion of knowledge: it gives people access to words but not to the understanding behind them, and unlike a living speaker, a text cannot answer questions or correct misreadings. The critique anticipates every subsequent anxiety about media technology — from the printing press to the internet — and the question it poses has never been answered: if the written word really is inferior to living conversation, what does that mean for philosophy, which now exists almost entirely in writing? Plato forces the reader to hold two things at once: the argument against the medium and the medium that delivers it.
